<reason>Side A secured victory by exposing a fatal contradiction in Side B's case: B claimed dynamic pricing helps budget-conscious locals find bargains, yet later conceded that general sales for marquee events are "a bloodbath of bots and speed" that locks buyers out—exactly the scenario the proposition addresses. A also dismantled B's verification argument by showing that B's preferred alternative (means-tested discounts) requires far more invasive income verification than the postal-code or membership checks A proposed. While B raised valid concerns about arbitrage and traveling fans, A answered these with plausible digital-ticketing mechanisms (non-transferable credentials, member reserves covering mobile fans) and direct A1/A2 responses to pressure questions. B's opening was clipped, and B struggled to recover from the concession that dynamic pricing fails during sell-out surges without resorting to a distinction (ordinary vs. marquee events) that effectively conceded the main ground.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange occurred in Rebuttal 2 and Closing when Side A weaponized Side B's own admission in [B2.5] that dynamic general sales are "a bloodbath of bots and speed." A contrasted this with B's earlier claim in [B1.6] that dynamic pricing lets locals buy "$50 bargains," forcing B to clarify in [B4.1] that dynamic pricing only works for ordinary events, not the large sell-out surges the proposition targets. This exposed that B's core defense of dynamic pricing collapses precisely when the policy would apply.</best_rebuttal>
